sections.h2: What deck and fence staining includes
body: A stain job is mostly prep. The stain itself goes on quickly; getting the wood ready to take it is where the time goes. Our deck and fence staining service covers the whole job, from cleaning off gray, weathered wood to fixing loose boards to the final coat. It covers walking surfaces, stairs, railings, pergolas, arbors, privacy fences, and picket fences.

This page explains the service and the choices you will make. If you want the details on why some stains fail quickly in our climate, how we pick a product system, and how often to recoat, see our companion page on deck and fence stain systems for Florida weather.
bullets: Cleaning and brightening, or stripping failed coatings
Sanding walking surfaces and handrails smooth
Replacing boards and pickets that are soft or split
Fixing loose rails, gates, and hardware
Stain applied by spray or roller and back-brushed into the grain

sections.h2: Choosing the look: transparent, semi-transparent, or solid
body: Transparent stains show nearly all the grain and give the wood a warm, natural tone. They look great on new or well-kept cedar, but they carry the least pigment, so they protect against sun the least and need recoating most often.

Semi-transparent stains are the middle ground most people end up choosing. Grain still shows, but color evens out boards that have weathered at different rates, and the added pigment holds up better in full sun.

Solid stains look closer to paint and hide the grain. They are a good fit for older decks and fences with mismatched replacement boards or staining from past finishes. On horizontal walking surfaces, we talk through wear before recommending a solid, since foot traffic shows on it sooner than on a fence.
We put samples on your own boards before deciding, because the same stain looks different on new pine, old pine, and cedar.

sections.h2: Decks vs. fences: different wood, different problems
body: A deck is the hardest-working wood on your property. It takes full sun, holds water at every screw, and dries fast enough to crack and cup. We sand the walking surface flat, set proud fasteners, and replace boards that probe soft. If you are seeing dark spots, spongy boards, or mushrooms near posts, read about the warning signs of deck wood rot before you book a stain.

Fences age unevenly. The sunny side fades and checks while the shaded side grows mildew. New pressure-treated pickets often still carry moisture from the mill and will not absorb stain until they dry out, so we either wait or use a product made for damp wood. Weathered fences need a cleaner and brightener so the color comes out even. Our post on treating a sun-damaged wood fence covers what to look for.

sections.h2: Stripping old finishes: when it is needed
body: Not every deck needs to be stripped. If the old stain was a penetrating product that has simply faded, a thorough clean and brightening is usually enough to accept a fresh coat. If the deck has a peeling film, a patchy solid stain, or a sealer that is flaking in the traffic paths, the old coating has to come off. New stain will not hold to a failing film underneath it, and patches of old finish will show through as blotches.

Stripping uses a chemical stripper made for exterior wood, followed by a neutralizing brightener and a rinse, then sanding where the surface has raised grain or splinters. It adds time to the job, and the estimate tells you up front whether your deck or fence needs it. Moving from a solid stain back to a semi-transparent is sometimes possible, but only if the old color strips cleanly; we test a small area before promising that look.

After the walkthrough, you get a written estimate listing the boards to be replaced, the prep method, the stain product and opacity, and the number of coats. Day one is usually cleaning; the wood then needs to dry before stain goes on, and we check moisture before we start. Most decks and fences are finished within a few working days of the wash, weather allowing. Plantings and siding next to the work are covered.

If you want other exterior wood treated at the same time, such as siding, shutters, or a front door, add it through our wood staining and finishing service. Local details are on our Gainesville deck staining and Ocala fence painting pages.

faqs.q: Should I choose transparent, semi-transparent, or solid stain?
faqs.a: Transparent shows the most grain but needs recoating soonest. Semi-transparent balances grain and sun protection and is the most common choice. Solid hides grain and mismatched boards and looks closer to paint. We test samples on your wood first.

faqs.q: Do you replace bad deck boards before staining?
faqs.a: Yes. Boards and pickets that are soft, split, or rotted are replaced and listed on the estimate before any stain is applied.

faqs.q: Can you stain a new pressure-treated fence?
faqs.a: Yes, but new treated lumber is often too wet to absorb stain. We check moisture and either wait until it dries or use a product made for damp wood.

faqs.q: Do you stain pergolas and railings?
faqs.a: Yes. Pergolas, arbors, stairs, and railings are included when listed on the estimate, and railings can be finished in a different product than the walking surface.
